gloss_terse: to give birth, bring forth offspring or produce results
gloss_readable: This verb describes the act of giving birth or bringing something forth. In James, it appears in both literal biological context (sin giving birth to death) and metaphorical spiritual context (God bringing forth believers through the word of truth). The multilingual evidence shows consistent rendering as birth/generation language across Romance and Germanic languages, reflecting the term's foundation in biological reproduction applied theologically.

senses.1: Used metaphorically in James 1:15 where sin 'brings forth' death, and literally in 1:18 where God 'gave birth to' believers through the word. The Greek middle/passive forms suggest both active birthing and being born, mirroring the dual biological process. Cross-linguistic glosses uniformly employ birth/generation terminology (Spanish 'engendra', German 'gebären'), confirming the physiological semantic core.

gloss_terse: enjoyment, the experience or result of enjoying something
gloss_readable: A noun denoting the act of enjoying or the pleasure derived from something. Paul uses it in 1 Timothy 6:17 to describe God's provision of all things for our enjoyment, while Hebrews 11:25 speaks of Moses refusing the fleeting enjoyment of sin. The classical range includes both the activity of enjoying and the concrete benefit received. All four languages represented (English, Spanish, French, German) converge on enjoyment/pleasure terminology, with German and French both using 'Genuss'.

senses.1: Appears in contexts contrasting earthly pleasures (1 Tim 6:17 - legitimate enjoyment of God's gifts; Heb 11:25 - temporary pleasure of sin). The term carries no inherent moral judgment; context determines whether the enjoyment is proper or improper. Classical Greek uses it for advantage or fruit gained from something, which fits Paul's emphasis on God richly providing things for our benefit.

gloss_terse: to wash away, cleanse by washing
gloss_readable: A compound verb meaning to wash off or wash away completely. In Acts 22:16, Ananias commands Saul to wash away his sins through baptism. In 1 Corinthians 6:11, Paul reminds the Corinthians they were washed clean from their former sinful state. Homer used it for washing gore or brine from the body; the New Testament applies this physical cleansing metaphorically to spiritual purification. The middle voice emphasizes washing oneself or having oneself washed.

senses.1: Both occurrences connect water baptism with spiritual cleansing (Acts 22:16; 1 Cor 6:11). The Greek middle voice in both passages suggests personal agency in receiving cleansing rather than purely passive reception. Multilingual evidence shows direct washing terminology across languages, though German preserves the actual Greek forms, suggesting recognition of this as technical baptismal vocabulary.

gloss_terse: to lead astray, cause to wander from truth or right path
gloss_readable: A verb describing the act of causing someone to go astray or be deceived. Jesus warns in Mark 13:22 that false messiahs will attempt to lead astray even the elect. Paul in 1 Timothy 6:10 describes how love of money has led some believers away from the faith. Classical usage includes both physical wandering and intellectual digression from truth. The compound emphasizes the notion of straying away from a proper position or belief.

senses.1: Used exclusively in contexts of spiritual or theological deviation (Mark 13:22 - deception by false prophets; 1 Tim 6:10 - wandering from faith). The passive forms in both passages indicate being led astray by external forces (deceptive signs, greed). Spanish 'engañar' emphasizes the deception aspect, while German 'abirren' captures the notion of going off course, both valid dimensions of the Greek term.

gloss_terse: to choke, suffocate, or drown
gloss_readable: A vivid verb describing suffocation or drowning. Both New Testament occurrences appear in Luke's account of the parable of the sower, where thorns choke the growing seed (Luke 8:7) and demons drive a herd of pigs to drown in a lake (8:33). Classical Greek employed it for throttling, choking on food, or drowning. The prefix intensifies the basic meaning of strangling to complete suffocation or death by choking.

senses.1: Appears only in Luke 8 in two distinct but related contexts: plants being choked by thorns (v.7) and pigs drowning in water (v.33). Both involve death by restriction of air. The agricultural metaphor relies on listeners' familiarity with thorns literally strangling crops. The multilingual glosses distinguish between choking (thorns) and drowning (pigs), showing translators recognized the different physical mechanisms while preserving the core semantic of life cut off through constriction.

gloss_terse: apostasy, rebellion against God, abandonment of faith
gloss_readable: A technical religious term denoting formal abandonment of faith or rebellion against God. In Acts 21:21, Paul is falsely accused of teaching Jews to commit apostasy from Moses. In 2 Thessalonians 2:3, Paul warns that the day of the Lord will not come until 'the apostasy' occurs. While classical Greek used it broadly for political rebellion or physical departure, biblical usage narrows it to religious defection. The Septuagint already employed it for rebellion against God, establishing its theological freight before the New Testament.

senses.1: Both occurrences carry severe theological weight - abandoning the covenant (Acts 21:21) or eschatological rebellion (2 Thess 2:3). The definite article in 2 Thessalonians ('the apostasy') suggests a specific, recognizable end-times revolt. Remarkably, all four target languages simply transliterate the Greek term rather than translate it, indicating 'apostasy' has become a fixed technical term in Christian theology across linguistic boundaries.

gloss_terse: to complete, accomplish, bring to fulfillment
gloss_readable: A verb meaning to bring to completion or accomplish fully. Jesus in Luke 13:32 speaks of completing his work on the third day. James 1:15 describes sin, when fully matured, giving birth to death. Classical usage emphasizes finishing what was started, paying what is due, or producing a final result. The compound suggests thorough completion, bringing something from beginning to final end.

senses.1: Used for processes reaching their intended culmination: Jesus' earthly ministry (Luke 13:32) and sin's deadly trajectory (James 1:15). Both passages emphasize temporal completion - Jesus on 'the third day', sin when 'full-grown'. The perfect passive participle in Luke suggests a state of completion, while the active present in James indicates ongoing accomplishment of sin's purpose. Cross-linguistic renderings emphasize both finishing (Spanish 'completado') and active accomplishment (Spanish 'realizo').

gloss_terse: to shake off, shake away from oneself
gloss_readable: A vivid gesture-verb describing the act of shaking something off one's body. Jesus instructs his disciples to shake dust off their feet as a testimony against towns that reject them (Luke 9:5). Paul shakes a viper off his hand into the fire on Malta (Acts 28:5). The middle voice emphasizes personal action - shaking off from oneself. Classical authors used it for getting rid of burdens or unwanted things, including metaphorical ones.

senses.1: Both New Testament instances involve symbolic or dramatic physical gestures: shaking off dust as prophetic testimony of rejection (Luke 9:5) and shaking off a deadly snake (Acts 28:5). The multilingual glosses uniformly preserve the physical action of shaking/shuddering off. Interestingly, the term appears in the Attitudes/Emotions domain despite its physical nature, perhaps because dust-shaking carries emotional freight as a gesture of disassociation and judgment.

gloss_terse: severity, sternness, harshness in treatment
gloss_readable: A noun denoting severity or harshness. Paul uses it twice in Romans 11:22 in a chiastic structure contrasting God's kindness and severity - severity toward those who fell, kindness toward those who continue in his kindness. The term carries connotations of cutting decisiveness, derived from the root for sharp cutting. Classical usage included harsh treatment, strict laws, or even torture. Paul's usage emphasizes God's uncompromising judgment alongside his mercy.

senses.1: Appears exclusively in Romans 11:22 where Paul contrasts divine kindness (χρηστότης) with divine severity. The context involves God cutting off unfaithful Israel from the olive tree - making the severity both metaphorical (judgment) and connected to literal cutting. The domain assignment to Plants/Agriculture is puzzling but may reflect the horticultural metaphor of the chapter (pruning branches). All four language witnesses use severity/sternness vocabulary, confirming the judicial rather than agricultural core meaning.

gloss_terse: severely, sharply, with cutting sternness
gloss_readable: An adverb meaning severely or sharply. Paul uses it twice to describe how he might exercise apostolic authority - sharply in 2 Corinthians 13:10 and commanding Titus to rebuke Cretans sharply (Titus 1:13). The term derives from the same root as 'severity' (G0663), carrying connotations of cutting decisiveness. It describes tone and manner of rebuke or correction that is direct and unsparing rather than gentle.

senses.1: Both occurrences involve apostolic discipline: Paul's potential sharp exercise of authority (2 Cor 13:10) and instruction to Titus to rebuke sharply (Tit 1:13). The adverb modifies verbs of rebuke/correction, emphasizing manner rather than content. The placement in the Power/Force domain reflects that sharp rebuke is an exercise of authority. French preserves the Greek term directly, while other languages employ native severity terminology, showing this is recognized as a specialized term for forceful correction.

gloss_terse: to separate, part from, be divided from
gloss_readable: A verb describing separation or division. In Acts 15:39, it describes the sharp disagreement that separated Paul and Barnabas. In Revelation 6:14, the sky is split apart and separated like a scroll being rolled up. The passive voice indicates being separated by external forces or circumstances. Classical usage included separating wheat from chaff, setting things apart into categories, or vomiting (forcible separation).

senses.1: The two occurrences show different applications of separation: relational parting between co-workers (Acts 15:39) and cosmic splitting of the heavens (Rev 6:14). Both are passive - the separation happens to the subjects rather than being actively chosen. Multilingual evidence consistently uses separation vocabulary, with German and French both preserving forms of the Greek root, suggesting recognition of this as a technical term. The domain of Whole/Unite/Part/Divide aptly captures the semantic of unity being undone.

gloss_terse: Arabia, the Arabian peninsula or region
gloss_readable: A geographical proper name referring to the Arabian peninsula or broader Arabian territory. Paul mentions going to Arabia in Galatians 1:17 after his conversion and before returning to Damascus. In Galatians 4:25, he makes a typological connection between Hagar, Mount Sinai, and Arabia. Classical Greek writers used the term for the Arabian lands, often associated with trade routes and desert regions. The Septuagint established the connection between Arabia and Sinai's location.

senses.1: Both occurrences in Galatians connect Arabia to significant locations in Paul's theology: his post-conversion retreat (1:17) and the Sinai covenant geography (4:25). The latter reference is particularly significant as Paul places Mount Sinai 'in Arabia,' showing his geographical understanding differed from later Christian tradition that located Sinai in the modern Sinai peninsula. All language witnesses simply transliterate 'Arabia,' as is standard for proper geographical names.

gloss_terse: men who engage in homosexual acts
gloss_readable: A compound noun literally meaning 'male-bedders,' referring to men who engage in sexual relations with males. Paul includes this term in two vice lists (1 Corinthians 6:9; 1 Timothy 1:10) among practices incompatible with the kingdom of God or sound doctrine. The term appears rarely in Greek literature, always with negative connotation. Classical usage referred to pederasty or male prostitution, though the precise scope remains debated among scholars.

senses.1: Both Pauline occurrences embed the term in catalogs of serious vices. In 1 Corinthians 6:9 it follows 'effeminate' (μαλακοί) in what may be a pair referring to passive and active partners. In 1 Timothy 1:10 it appears in a list drawn from the Decalogue's moral framework. Modern translations struggle with precision, as evidenced by the multilingual glosses using generic 'homosexuals' terminology. The German 'Knabenschänder' (boy-violator) reflects older interpretation focusing on pederastic abuse specifically.

gloss_terse: archangel, a chief or ruling angel
gloss_readable: A term meaning chief angel or archangel, denoting a high-ranking angelic being. Paul mentions the archangel's voice announcing Christ's return (1 Thessalonians 4:16). Jude refers to 'Michael the archangel' disputing with the devil over Moses' body (Jude 1:9). The compound combines 'ruler/chief' with 'angel,' indicating hierarchical structure in the angelic realm. Jewish apocalyptic literature developed elaborate angelologies featuring archangels as leaders of heavenly hosts.

senses.1: The two New Testament occurrences present the archangel in eschatological and spiritual warfare contexts. In 1 Thessalonians, the archangel's shout accompanies Christ's parousia. In Jude, Michael the archangel models restraint even when contending with Satan, refusing to pronounce blasphemous judgment. The term is universally transliterated across languages (Spanish 'arcángel', French 'archange', German 'Erzengel'), showing it has become standardized theological vocabulary.

gloss_terse: Archippus, a Christian co-worker of Paul
gloss_readable: A proper name meaning 'master of horse' or 'horse-ruler,' referring to a Christian associated with Paul's circle. Paul greets Archippus in Colossians 4:17, urging him to fulfill the ministry he received in the Lord. In Philemon 1:2, Paul calls him 'our fellow soldier,' indicating close partnership in gospel work. The military language suggests Archippus faced opposition or difficult ministry circumstances. His exact role and location remain unclear, though connection to Colossae seems likely.

senses.1: Both references come from the Colossian correspondence. The exhortation in Colossians 4:17 to 'complete' or 'fulfill' his ministry suggests either Archippus faced discouragement or needed reminder of responsibility. The 'fellow soldier' designation in Philemon indicates Paul saw him as frontline ministry partner, not mere adherent. All language witnesses transliterate the name with minor phonetic variation reflecting each language's orthography.

gloss_terse: to rule, govern, exercise authority over
gloss_readable: A verb meaning to rule, lead, or exercise authority. Jesus notes that Gentile rulers lord it over their subjects (Mark 10:42). Paul quotes Isaiah's prophecy that the root of Jesse will rise 'to rule over the Gentiles' (Romans 15:12). Classical usage encompassed beginning/leading and ruling/commanding - being first in time or first in authority. The New Testament occurrences focus exclusively on the governance sense.

senses.1: Both passages address ruling over the nations/Gentiles but with contrasting tones. In Mark 10:42, Jesus critiques how Gentile rulers 'lord it over' subjects, using this as a negative example. In Romans 15:12, Christ's rule over Gentiles is the prophetic hope. The semantic range includes legitimate governance and oppressive domination - context determines valence. Multilingual glosses uniformly use govern/rule terminology across all four languages.

gloss_terse: Asaph, a name appearing in Matthew's genealogy
gloss_readable: A Hebrew name (meaning 'collector' or 'gatherer') appearing in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. Modern critical editions recognize this as likely a textual corruption of 'Asa,' the king of Judah (1 Kings 15). The confusion may have arisen because Asaph was a famous Levitical musician and psalmist (Psalms 73-83), making the name familiar to scribes. Most translations follow manuscripts that read 'Asa' rather than 'Asaph.'

senses.1: Both Matthew 1:7-8 references locate this figure in the royal genealogy between Abijah and Jehoshaphat, the position occupied by King Asa in the biblical narrative. The textual variant reflects how manuscript transmission could introduce familiar names in place of less common ones. Modern translation evidence (French 'Asa', German 'Asa') shows most translators adopt the reading 'Asa,' treating 'Asaph' as scribal error despite appearing in several Greek manuscripts.

gloss_terse: unshakable, immovable, firmly fixed
gloss_readable: An adjective meaning unable to be shaken or moved. In Acts 27:41, it describes the bow of Paul's shipwrecked vessel becoming stuck fast in the seabed. In Hebrews 12:28, believers receive an unshakable kingdom. The term combines the negative prefix with a verb meaning 'to shake,' producing the sense of stability against external forces. Classical usage applied it to Delos (mythically fixed by Zeus) and to unshakeable faith or ordinances.

senses.1: The two occurrences demonstrate literal (Acts 27:41 - ship stuck firmly) and metaphorical (Hebrews 12:28 - kingdom that cannot be shaken) applications. Both emphasize resistance to external forces attempting to move or destabilize. The Hebrews passage contrasts this unshakeable kingdom with shakeable created things being removed. All language witnesses use un-movable or un-shakeable constructions, preserving the Greek negative formation.

gloss_terse: Asher, a Hebrew patriarch and tribal ancestor
gloss_readable: A Hebrew name (meaning 'happy' or 'blessed') referring to Jacob's eighth son and the tribe descended from him. In Luke 2:36, Anna the prophetess is identified as from the tribe of Asher. In Revelation 7:6, the tribe of Asher is listed among the 144,000 sealed from the twelve tribes. Asher's territory was in northern Israel along the Mediterranean coast. The name is indeclinable in Greek, maintaining its Hebrew form.

senses.1: Both New Testament occurrences use Asher as a tribal identifier rather than referring to the patriarch himself. Anna's tribal affiliation (Luke 2:36) is one of the few specific tribal identities mentioned in the New Testament, showing preservation of genealogical memory. The Revelation 7:6 listing includes all twelve tribes in symbolic completeness. All languages transliterate the name with minor phonetic variation (German 'Asser', French 'Aser', Spanish 'Asēr').

gloss_terse: assarion, a small Roman copper coin worth about 1/16 denarius
gloss_readable: A loanword from Latin denoting a small copper coin of minimal value. Jesus uses it in sayings about God's care for sparrows: two sparrows sold for an assarion (Matthew 10:29), five for two assaria (Luke 12:6). The point is that even creatures of negligible economic worth are noticed by the Father. The assarion was roughly equivalent to 1/16 of a denarius (a day's wage), making it a coin of very small purchasing power.

senses.1: Both Gospel occurrences employ the assarion in identical proverbial logic: sparrows cost very little in the market, yet God knows each one. Luke's version intensifies the point - five sparrows for two assaria shows buyers get a 'free' fifth sparrow, yet none are forgotten. The Latin loanword appears across language families, with French 'as' and Spanish 'ases' adapting the Latin, while German preserves the Greek form, showing varying degrees of naturalization.

gloss_terse: Assos, a seaport city in the Roman province of Asia
gloss_readable: A Greek city on the northwest coast of Asia Minor (modern Turkey), located on the southern shore of the Gulf of Adramyttium. Acts 20:13-14 describes Paul's travel itinerary: his companions sailed from Troas to Assos while Paul went by land, meeting them there before continuing to Mitylene. The land route was about 20 miles shorter than sailing around Cape Lectum. Assos was known for its steep acropolis and sarcophagi made from local stone.

senses.1: Both Acts references (20:13-14) narrate the same event from slightly different angles: the plan to meet at Assos (v.13) and its fulfillment (v.14). Paul's decision to walk while others sailed may have been for pastoral reasons (visiting believers) or personal preference for land travel. All language witnesses transliterate the city name uniformly, with German using 'Ἆσσον' showing the accusative case form that appears in the Greek text.

gloss_terse: beautiful, fair, elegant, pleasing to look at
gloss_readable: An adjective meaning beautiful, elegant, or pleasing in appearance. Stephen is described as 'beautiful to God' as an infant (Acts 7:20). Moses' parents saw he was 'a beautiful child' and hid him from Pharaoh (Hebrews 11:23). Classical usage ranged from 'of the town/urbane' to 'refined/witty' to general praise for beauty. The New Testament uses it exclusively for physical attractiveness, specifically of infants whose appearance moved their parents to protective action.

senses.1: Both occurrences describe Moses as an exceptionally beautiful baby (Acts 7:20; Heb 11:23). Acts uses the striking phrase 'beautiful to God' (ἀστεῖος τῷ θεῷ), suggesting divine approval beyond mere physical appearance. This beauty motivated his parents to extraordinary measures of protection. The multilingual witnesses uniformly translate with beauty terminology, though this Greek word could also mean 'urbane' or 'witty' in classical contexts - senses not evidenced in the New Testament.

gloss_terse: unstable, unsettled, not firmly established
gloss_readable: An adjective meaning unstable or not firmly fixed. Peter warns that unstable people distort Scripture to their destruction (2 Peter 2:14; 3:16). The term combines a negative prefix with a verb meaning 'to fix firmly' or 'prop up,' yielding the sense of lacking firm foundation. It can describe physical instability (not supported) or moral/spiritual instability (lacking grounding). Peter uses it exclusively for spiritual instability - people susceptible to false teaching.

senses.1: Both occurrences in 2 Peter describe the same category of people: those unstable in faith who are vulnerable to distorting Paul's letters and other Scriptures (3:16) and who are enticed by false teachers (2:14). The term suggests not active rebellion but rather lack of firm grounding that makes one easily swayed. All four language witnesses use 'unstable/inconstant' terminology, with French and German preserving forms closer to the Greek root.

gloss_terse: without natural affection, lacking family love
gloss_readable: An adjective describing people devoid of natural family affection. Paul lists it among the vices characterizing godlessness in the last days (Romans 1:31; 2 Timothy 3:3). The term negates 'storge,' the Greek word for family affection and parental love. It describes the chilling absence of instinctive bonds that normally tie families together - parents who don't love children, children who don't care for parents. Classical usage applied it to cruel or heartless behavior.

senses.1: Both Pauline vice catalogs include this term among society's moral breakdowns. Romans 1:31 places it in a list of characteristics of those who suppress truth about God. 2 Timothy 3:3 warns Timothy about people in 'last days' exhibiting this heartlessness. The absence of natural affection represents profound moral degradation - the dissolution of foundational human bonds. German 'lieblos' (loveless) and French 'sans-affection' (without affection) capture the privative sense.

gloss_terse: to flash, shine brightly like lightning
gloss_readable: A verb meaning to flash or gleam like lightning. Jesus describes his coming as lightning that flashes from east to west (Luke 17:24). At the resurrection, two men in dazzling apparel appear to the women (Luke 24:4). Classical usage described lightning bolts, gleaming weapons or armor, and shining faces. The New Testament employs it for supernatural radiance associated with divine presence or eschatological events.

senses.1: Both Lukan occurrences involve heavenly brilliance. In Luke 17:24, Jesus uses lightning's sudden visibility across the sky as a metaphor for the unmistakable nature of his coming. In Luke 24:4, the angelic beings' dazzling clothing signals heavenly origin. The present participles in both passages emphasize continuous flashing/shining rather than single flash. Cross-linguistic glosses employ lightning and brilliance terminology, with German preserving the Greek forms, suggesting technical recognition.

gloss_terse: to behave improperly or indecently
gloss_readable: A verb meaning to act in an unseemly or improper manner. Paul uses it regarding a man who might be acting improperly toward his betrothed (1 Corinthians 7:36). He also says love 'does not behave indecently' (1 Corinthians 13:5). The term derives from a negative prefix and 'schema' (form/appearance), suggesting behavior that violates proper form or decorum. Classical usage included disgraceful conduct or bringing discredit.

senses.1: The two Corinthian occurrences address different applications: potential sexual impropriety in engagement (7:36) and general standard for love's behavior (13:5). The first passage is notoriously difficult - Paul may be addressing a father, a man and his fiancée, or spiritual marriage. The second establishes that genuine love observes proper boundaries and respect. Multilingual renderings emphasize impropriety and indecency, though the domain assignment to Value (Economics/Property) seems unexpected.

gloss_terse: shameful behavior, indecency, private parts (euphemism)
gloss_readable: A noun denoting shameful or indecent behavior, or euphemistically referring to private parts. Paul describes homosexual acts as 'shameless acts' or 'indecency' (Romans 1:27). Revelation 16:15 warns about walking naked and having one's shame exposed. Classical usage ranged from lack of grace or awkwardness to moral impropriety to euphemistic reference to genitals. The Septuagint used it for nakedness or shameful exposure.

senses.1: The two occurrences span the semantic range: sexual immorality (Rom 1:27) and shameful exposure/nakedness (Rev 16:15). Romans emphasizes the shamelessness of the acts themselves. Revelation uses clothing imagery for spiritual vigilance, where nakedness represents unprepared shame. The Septuagint background of this term as euphemism for genitals informs both passages. Multilingual evidence shows 'shame/indecency' as the primary rendering across all four languages.

gloss_terse: in a disorderly manner, without proper discipline
gloss_readable: An adverb meaning in a disorderly, undisciplined, or irregular manner. Paul warns the Thessalonians not to associate with believers walking disorderly (2 Thessalonians 3:6, 11). The context indicates people not working but being busybodies. The root word described soldiers out of formation, irregular rhythms in music or medicine, or generally undisciplined behavior. Paul's usage focuses on Christians who violate community standards regarding work and mutual responsibility.

senses.1: Both uses in 2 Thessalonians 3 address the same issue: believers living in disorderly fashion by refusing to work and interfering in others' affairs (v.6, 11). The military metaphor of being 'out of ranks' fits Paul's self-description of working night and day as an example. French preserves the Greek form directly while other languages use disorder terminology. The domain of Relations captures how this disorder disrupts proper community order.

gloss_terse: without, apart from, in the absence of
gloss_readable: A preposition meaning without or apart from, taking the genitive case. Jesus asks his disciples to recall being sent out 'without purse' (Luke 22:35). Judas sought to betray Jesus 'without a crowd' or 'away from the multitude' (Luke 22:6). Epic and tragic poetry used this term where classical prose preferred 'choris' or 'aneu.' It emphasizes complete absence or separation from something normally expected or present.

senses.1: Luke employs this somewhat archaic preposition twice in chapter 22. In verse 35, Jesus reminds disciples of their prior mission without provisions, establishing precedent for dependence on God and hospitality. In verse 6, it describes Judas's strategy of betraying Jesus away from the crowds who might have intervened. Most modern languages use simple 'without' constructions, with German preserving the Greek form, showing recognition of this as a distinctive term.

gloss_terse: vapor, mist, exhalation, steam
gloss_readable: A noun denoting moist vapor, steam, or mist rising from heated liquid. Peter quotes Joel's prophecy of 'blood and fire and vapor of smoke' accompanying the day of the Lord (Acts 2:19). James compares human life to a vapor that appears briefly then vanishes (James 4:14). Classical usage distinguished moist vapor (atmis) from dry smoke (kapnos), though they could combine. The term emphasizes transience and insubstantiality.

senses.1: The two occurrences illustrate different applications: eschatological signs (Acts 2:19) and wisdom teaching about life's brevity (James 4:14). In Acts, vapor of smoke is part of cosmic upheaval. In James, vapor serves as metaphor for life's fleeting nature - visible momentarily then gone. Both leverage the physical property of vapor as transient and insubstantial. All four languages use vapor/steam terminology, recognizing the physical phenomenon underlying both literal and metaphorical uses.

gloss_terse: self-willed, arrogant, stubborn, pleased with oneself
gloss_readable: An adjective describing someone who is self-willed, arrogant, or stubbornly insistent on their own way. Paul lists it among qualifications an overseer must not have (Titus 1:7). Peter warns of bold and self-willed people who are not afraid to blaspheme (2 Peter 2:10). The term combines 'self' and 'pleasing,' suggesting someone who pleases only themselves with no regard for others. Classical usage included stubborn, surly, or self-pleasing senses.

senses.1: Both occurrences describe people in positions of influence who wrongly assert their will: disqualified church leaders (Titus 1:7) and false teachers (2 Pet 2:10). The term captures the opposite of other-centered humility - these people operate from self-centered arrogance. Paul contrasts this with the servant-hearted leadership required in God's household. Multilingual glosses use arrogant/self-willed terminology across languages, with French and German preserving forms closer to the Greek.

gloss_terse: of one's own accord, voluntary, self-chosen
gloss_readable: An adjective meaning done of one's own free choice or voluntary initiative. Paul describes the Macedonians' generosity as being of their own accord (2 Corinthians 8:3, 17). The term combines 'self' and 'chosen,' emphasizing voluntary action rather than compulsion. Classical usage applied it to self-elected magistrates, voluntary service, or self-incurred consequences. Paul uses it positively for freely chosen generosity that exceeds external pressure.

senses.1: Both occurrences in 2 Corinthians 8 commend voluntary generosity. In verse 3, the Macedonians gave beyond their ability 'of their own accord,' not under Paul's pressure. In verse 17, Titus went to Corinth 'of his own accord,' showing initiative. The term emphasizes the internal motivation and freedom characterizing genuine Christian giving and service. Cross-linguistic evidence shows 'of own accord/free will' renderings, with German 'freiwillig' (freely willing) capturing the voluntary essence.

gloss_terse: flute-player, one who plays the aulos (reed instrument)
gloss_readable: A noun denoting someone who plays the aulos, a double-reed wind instrument similar to an oboe. Jesus encounters flute-players at Jairus's house performing customary mourning music (Matthew 9:23). Revelation's lament over Babylon includes the silencing of flute-players among other musicians (Revelation 18:22). Flute-players were common at funerals and festivals in the ancient world. The Greek term could also refer to certain wasps or sanitary engineers in specialized texts.

senses.1: Both New Testament references place flute-players in contexts of public events: funeral mourning (Matt 9:23) and the cessation of city life (Rev 18:22). Matthew specifically notes the noise and crowd accompanying the professional mourners with their flutes. Revelation's prophecy of silenced musicians symbolizes complete desolation. All language witnesses use flute-player terminology, recognizing this as a professional class of musicians rather than casual performers.

gloss_terse: to spend the night, lodge, camp for the night
gloss_readable: A verb meaning to pass the night, lodge, or encamp. Jesus lodged at Bethany during his final week (Matthew 21:17). Luke notes Jesus spent nights on the Mount of Olives while teaching in the temple by day (Luke 21:37). The term originally referred to staying in a courtyard (aule), then broadened to any overnight lodging or military encampment. Classical usage included sheep lying down in folds, birds roosting, or armies bivouacking.

senses.1: Both Gospel occurrences describe Jesus' lodging pattern during Passion Week: staying in Bethany (Matt 21:17) or on the Mount of Olives (Luke 21:37) while teaching daily in Jerusalem's temple. The imperfect tense in Matthew emphasizes habitual action - Jesus repeatedly lodged there. The pattern shows Jesus avoided staying in potentially hostile Jerusalem at night. Cross-linguistic glosses uniformly use lodging/spending-night terminology, with German preserving Greek forms showing recognition of this as a technical term for overnight stay.

gloss_terse: growth, increase in size or maturity
gloss_readable: A noun denoting growth or increase. Paul describes the body of Christ growing through what every part supplies, making 'growth of the body' (Ephesians 4:16; Colossians 2:19). The term appears in botanical contexts in classical Greek for physical growth of plants or mathematical increments. Paul applies it metaphorically to the church's development toward maturity. The emphasis is on organic increase rather than mechanical addition.

senses.1: Both Pauline occurrences use identical phrasing about the body's growth (τὴν αὔξησιν τοῦ σώματος) in parallel passages about Christ as head and the church as body. Ephesians 4:16 emphasizes each part's contribution to growth. Colossians 2:19 stresses growth that comes from God. The biological metaphor of growth fits Paul's body imagery. French preserves the Greek term directly while other languages use native growth vocabulary, showing varying degrees of terminological standardization.

gloss_terse: harsh, severe, stern, austere
gloss_readable: An adjective meaning harsh, severe, or austere. Jesus quotes a servant who feared his master as 'a harsh man' who reaps where he didn't sow (Luke 19:21-22). The term derives from a root meaning 'to dry up,' and classical usage included harsh wine (opposed to sweet), rough terrain, or severe personalities. It describes someone exacting and demanding, showing no leniency. Jesus uses it to expose the servant's false perception that led to paralysis rather than productivity.

senses.1: Both occurrences in Luke 19 appear in the same parable dialogue - the servant's accusation (v.21) and the master's response using the servant's own words (v.22). The servant claims fear of the harsh master excuses his inaction, but the master shows this very logic should have motivated banking the money. The term characterizes perceived rather than actual harshness. All four language witnesses use harsh/severe terminology, with German preserving the Greek forms.

gloss_terse: self-sufficiency, contentment, competence, adequate resources
gloss_readable: A noun denoting self-sufficiency or contentment with what one has. Paul speaks of God providing sufficiency so believers abound in good works (2 Corinthians 9:8). He commends godliness with contentment as great gain (1 Timothy 6:6). Classical philosophy, especially Stoicism, prized autarkeia as the ideal of needing nothing external. Paul transforms this virtue: Christian contentment depends not on internal resources but on God's provision.

senses.1: The two Pauline occurrences show different nuances. In 2 Corinthians 9:8, 'sufficiency' or 'all you need' emphasizes God supplying adequate resources for generosity. In 1 Timothy 6:6, 'contentment' emphasizes satisfaction with what one has rather than craving more. Both contrast with self-reliant Stoic autarkeia by grounding sufficiency in divine provision. German 'Genügsamkeit' (enough-ness) captures the contentment aspect while 'sufficiency' captures the adequacy aspect.

gloss_terse: by itself, of its own accord, spontaneously
gloss_readable: An adjective meaning self-acting or spontaneous, often used adverbially. Jesus describes seed sprouting and growing automatically in Mark 4:28 - the earth produces crops 'by itself.' In Acts 12:10, the prison gate opens 'of its own accord' as Peter is led out by the angel. Classical usage included self-moving tripods, automatic gates of Olympus, and plants growing wild without cultivation. The term emphasizes action without external human agency.

senses.1: Both New Testament occurrences involve processes happening without human intervention: crop growth (Mark 4:28) and miraculous gate-opening (Acts 12:10). Mark's parable emphasizes the mysterious autonomy of growth - farmers plant and harvest but cannot control the growth process itself. Acts emphasizes divine action making the gate open on its own. Cross-linguistic glosses uniformly use 'of itself/by itself' constructions, preserving the auto- (self) semantic core across all languages.

gloss_terse: latrine, toilet, privy, place of defecation
gloss_readable: A noun denoting a latrine or privy. Jesus teaches that food enters the stomach and goes out into the latrine (Matthew 15:17; Mark 7:19). The term derives from 'hedra' (seat), with the prefix suggesting a place set apart. It was a euphemistic way to refer to the toilet. Jesus uses it in teaching that external things cannot defile since they pass through the digestive system and are expelled, making the point that moral defilement comes from the heart.

senses.1: Both occurrences appear in the same teaching about clean and unclean (Matt 15:17; Mark 7:19). Jesus traces food's path: mouth → stomach → latrine, demonstrating that food doesn't enter the heart and therefore can't morally defile. Mark adds the editorial comment that Jesus thus declared all foods clean. The parallel passages show this was core teaching about the source of defilement. All four languages use latrine/toilet terminology, handling this delicate subject with similar euphemistic restraint.

gloss_terse: ligament, joint, bond connecting body parts
gloss_readable: A noun denoting a ligament, joint, or connection between body parts. Paul uses it metaphorically twice for how Christ's body (the church) is held together and grows through what every ligament supplies (Ephesians 4:16; Colossians 2:19). Classical usage included the sense of touch, grip in wrestling, contact of surfaces in mathematics, and sand for wrestlers to get better grip. The anatomical sense of connecting tissue fits Paul's body ecclesiology.

senses.1: Both occurrences appear in nearly identical contexts about the body being supported and knit together through every supporting ligament (Eph 4:16; Col 2:19). Paul's metaphor emphasizes that church unity and growth depend on proper connections - each member functioning in relationship with others. The genitive plural form suggests multiple connection points throughout the body. French and German preserve Greek forms, showing recognition of this as Pauline technical terminology for ecclesial anatomy.
